aspects.keyword_query: strategy rationale affiliation choice value proposition competitive advantage flexibility attracting advisors growth strategy

a1.RJF.label: fact

items.text: Raymond James's AdvisorChoice® platform offers multiple affiliation options that financial advisors can choose from, each with a unique combination of support, freedom and flexibility: Traditional Employee, Advisor Select, Independent Contractor, Bank & Credit Union, and Corporate RIA.
items.quote: Through AdvisorChoice®, you have the ability to match your professional goals to the affiliation option that's right for you... Traditional Employee... Advisor Select... Independent Contractor... Bank & Credit Union... Corporate RIA

items.text: Raymond James offers multiple affiliation options under AdvisorChoice®, and financial advisors primarily affiliate directly as either employees or independent contractors, or as employees of third-party RIAs and broker-dealers served through its RIA and Custody Services (RCS) division.
items.quote: We offer multiple affiliation options, which we refer to as AdvisorChoice®. Financial advisors primarily affiliate with us directly as either employees or independent contractors or as employees of third-party Registered Investment Advisors ("RIAs") and broker-dealers to which we provide services through our RIA and Custody Services ("RCS") division.

items.text: Employee financial advisors work in a traditional branch supported by local management and administrative staff, provide services predominantly to retail clients, and receive compensation primarily as a payout on revenues they generate plus participation in the firm's employee benefit plans.
items.quote: Employee financial advisors work in a traditional branch supported by local management and administrative staff. They provide services predominantly to retail clients. Compensation for these financial advisors primarily includes a payout on revenues they generate and such advisors also participate in the firm's employee benefit plans.

items.text: Independent contractor financial advisors are generally responsible for all of their direct costs and accordingly receive a higher payout percentage on revenues than employee financial advisors; they may affiliate directly or through an affiliated bank or credit union in the Financial Institutions Division, and with approval may conduct certain other approved business activities such as insurance, independent RIA services, and accounting/tax services.
items.quote: Our financial advisors who are independent contractors are generally responsible for all of their direct costs and, accordingly, receive a higher payout percentage on the revenues they generate than employee financial advisors... Independent contractor financial advisors may affiliate with us directly or through an affiliated bank or credit union in our Financial Institutions Division.

items.text: The AdvisorChoice spectrum spans Employee (RJA), Advisor Select, Independent Advisor (ICD), Banks and Credit Unions, IAR (Corporate RIA), and RIA & Custody Services, and the firm states the movement to 'independence' is not channel-specific.
items.quote: EMPLOYEE ADVISOR (RJA) — ADVISOR SELECT — INDEPENDENT ADVISOR (ICD) — BANKS AND CREDIT UNIONS — IAR* (CORPORATE RIA) — RIA** & CUSTODY SERVICES... The movement to "independence" is not channel-specific

items.text: As an independent contractor, an advisor can access Raymond James's full capabilities (private wealth, technology, marketing) while operating their own independent practice backed by a full-service, self-clearing NYSE-member broker/dealer.
items.quote: When you affiliate with Raymond James as an independent contractor, you can access our full capabilities at a level that's right for your business... Serve your clients and grow your independent practice... the support of a full-service, self-clearing New York Stock Exchange-member broker/dealer.

items.text: Advisor Select® is an employee affiliation option that provides established advisors the full benefits of the employee channel with the independence to create their own branches and run their branch's P&L to earn a higher rate on production.
items.quote: Advisor Select® provides established advisors the full benefits of our employee channel with the independence to create their own branches... run your branch's P&L to earn a higher rate on production. Advisor Select® is... an employee affiliation option

items.text: Through the RIA & Custody Services (RCS) division, an independent registered investment advisor (RIA) retains complete freedom and control of its business, using as much or as little of Raymond James's support as needed, with strategic, financial and administrative control free from retail conflict.
items.quote: As an independent registered investment advisor (RIA) with a committed custodian partner... Our RIA & Custody Services division gives you true strategic, financial and administrative control to grow your business your way, free from retail conflict and using as much - or as little - of our support as you need.

a1.RJF.reason: The passages directly describe the structure of the affiliation-choice model, including the employee and independent contractor options and the related Advisor Select, Bank & Credit Union, Corporate RIA, and RCS options.

a2.RJF.label: fact

items.text: Raymond James states that in its Traditional Employee affiliation model, advisors receive up to 50% payout plus a full array of competitive employee benefits offerings.
items.quote: Payout + Benefits: Up to 50% payout** and full array of competitive employee benefits offerings.

items.text: Raymond James states that in its Advisor Select affiliation model, advisors receive a 70-80% gross payout plus a full array of competitive employee benefits offerings.
items.quote: Payout + Benefits: 70-80% gross payout** and full array of competitive employee benefits offerings.

items.text: Raymond James states that in its Independent Contractor affiliation model, advisors receive an 81% to 90% payout, leveraging third-party partnerships to create a benefits package.
items.quote: Payout + Benefits: 81% to 90% payout***. Leverage our third party partnerships to create a benefits package that best fits your team.

items.text: Raymond James states that in its Corporate RIA affiliation model, advisors receive an 81% to 90% payout, leveraging third-party partnerships to create a benefits package.
items.quote: Payout + Benefits: 81% to 90% payout***. Leverage our third-party partnerships to create a benefits package that best fits your team.

items.text: Raymond James states that in its Bank & Credit Union affiliation model, advisors receive a competitive compensation package from the financial institution in partnership with Raymond James during their transition.
items.quote: Payout + Benefits: Get the support you need during your transition by receiving a competitive compensation package from the financial institution in partnership with Raymond James.

items.text: Raymond James states that in its RIA & Custody Services affiliation model, advisors work with their RIA or broker/dealer to determine compensation and create their own benefits package.
items.quote: Payout + Benefits: Work with your RIA or broker/dealer to determine compensation. Create your own benefits package.

items.text: Raymond James states that compensation for its employee financial advisors primarily includes a payout on revenues they generate, and such advisors also participate in the firm's employee benefit plans.
items.quote: Compensation for these financial advisors primarily includes a payout on revenues they generate and such advisors also participate in the firm's employee benefit plans.

items.text: Raymond James states that its independent contractor financial advisors are generally responsible for all of their direct costs and, accordingly, receive a higher payout percentage on the revenues they generate than employee financial advisors.
items.quote: Our financial advisors who are independent contractors are generally responsible for all of their direct costs and, accordingly, receive a higher payout percentage on the revenues they generate than employee financial advisors.

items.text: Raymond James's CEO explains that independent advisor payouts are higher than employee payouts because independent advisors cover their own overhead costs, real estate, and health insurance.
items.quote: the independent payouts are higher because they cover their overhead costs, their real estate, their health insurance, et cetera

items.text: Raymond James's CEO states that even on the employee side the firm has tiered payout systems, so as production increases advisors move higher up the payout grid.
items.quote: even on the employee side, we have tiered payout systems. And so as production increases, you kind of get higher up on the payout grid as well.

a2.RJF.reason: Passages state payout percentages, cost responsibilities, and economic differences by affiliation type, which is exactly what the sub-question asks.

a5.RJF.label: fact

items.text: CEO Paul Shoukry states Raymond James offers the largest addressable market in the industry because it has all the affiliation options an adviser could want, and is agnostic about how an adviser affiliates, wanting advisers to be drawn by the culture, values, platform and capabilities.
items.quote: we have the largest addressable market in the industry because we have all the affiliation options that an adviser could possibly want. And we have adviser choice where we're agnostic into how you affiliate with Raymond James. We want you to fall in love with our culture, values and the platform and capabilities and how you affiliate with us, we're indifferent to.

items.text: CEO Paul Shoukry states the firm does not lead with the highest check but with culture and capabilities, and that it has a true differentiated value proposition while remaining disciplined on transition assistance and economics to advisers.
items.quote: we don't lead with the highest check. We want to have competitive economics. Certainly, we have to have competitive economics, but we lead with culture and capabilities. And so we have a true differentiated value proposition.

items.text: CEO Paul Shoukry states the firm is focused on the long term and providing a stable platform, attracting and retaining financial advisors with its unique culture, leading service and robust platform rather than the largest check, and valuing independence.
items.quote: We are focused on the long-term and providing a stable platform for our advisors, bankers, and associates, whereas so many of our competitors are increasingly looking for an exit in three to five years or even less. We attract and retain financial advisors with our unique culture, leading service, and robust platform, whereas many of our competitors compete with the largest check.

items.text: CEO Paul Shoukry states the value proposition is having the largest addressable market across affiliation options, from employee to independent contractor to RIA custody, with critical mass and decades of experience in all of them.
items.quote: we have the largest addressable market across our affiliation options, from employee to independent contractor to the RIA custody, and we have critical mass and decades of experience in all of them. It's not a new venture for us.

items.text: CEO Paul Shoukry states advisers do not have to choose between culture and capabilities, as the firm offers a unique combination of an adviser- and client-focused culture with leading technology, products and solutions, combined with a strong balance sheet, long-term thinking and commitment to independence.
items.quote: At Raymond James, advisers do not have to choose between culture and capabilities. We offer a unique combination of an adviser and client-focused culture together with leading technologies, products and solutions advisers need to serve clients at a high level.

items.text: CEO Paul Shoukry states recruiting is a long-term process that cannot be dialed up or down quarter by quarter, and that the firm wants advisors who want to be there over the long term rather than those moving for the highest check.
items.quote: It's a marathon, not a sprint... if you dial up recruiting quarter by quarter or dial it down quarter by quarter, then you're not gonna get the quality advisors that you want... We have to have a competitive check, but we want the advisors that want to be here over the long term.

a5.RJF.reason: Management's strategic rationale and priorities for the affiliation-choice model are stated directly in these executive remarks, with no figures.

claims.text: In its fiscal 2025 Form 10-K (period ended September 30, 2025), Raymond James states it offers multiple affiliation options referred to as AdvisorChoice®, and that financial advisors primarily affiliate directly as either employees or independent contractors, or as employees of third-party registered investment advisors and broker-dealers served through its RIA and Custody Services (RCS) division.

In its fiscal 2025 Form 10-K (period ended September 30, 2025), Raymond James states that independent contractor financial advisors are generally responsible for all of their direct costs and accordingly receive a higher payout percentage on revenues than employee financial advisors; they may affiliate directly or through an affiliated bank or credit union in the Financial Institutions Division, and with approval may conduct other approved business activities such as insurance, independent RIA services, and accounting/tax services.

claims.text: Schwab's 2025 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025) states that its largest sources of net revenues are net interest revenue, asset management and administration fees, trading revenue, and bank deposit account fees, supported by the combination of its broker-dealer, bank, and asset management operating subsidiaries.

Schwab's 2025 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025) states that net interest revenue is the difference between interest generated on interest-earning assets and interest paid on funding sources; its primary funding source is uninvested client cash balances held on its balance sheet, and its interest-earning assets are primarily high-quality fixed income securities, margin loans, and bank loans.

Schwab's 2025 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025) states that asset management and administration fees are primarily earned from proprietary money market mutual funds, proprietary and third-party mutual funds and ETFs, and fee-based managed investing solutions.

Schwab's 2025 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025) states that trading revenue includes commissions earned for executing trades for clients in certain individual equities, options, futures, fixed income securities, and certain third-party mutual funds and ETFs; order flow revenue; and principal transactions revenue earned primarily from actions to support client trading in fixed income securities.

Schwab's 2025 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025) states that client cash balances are a significant funding source for generating revenue: cash awaiting investment may be used to extend margin loans to clients or be swept to its banking subsidiaries, and those bank deposits are then used to extend loans to clients and purchase investment securities.

Schwab's 2025 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025) states that bank deposit account fees consist of revenues resulting from sweep programs offered to certain clients whereby uninvested client cash is swept off-balance sheet to FDIC-insured accounts at the TD Depository Institutions, in exchange for which Schwab provides marketing, recordkeeping, and support services.

The comparison of revenue yield on client assets between Schwab and advisor-led models can be made only on the basis of Schwab's own investor-day presentation (Schwab's investor day deck, published May 14, 2026), which reports Schwab's revenue on client assets at approximately 21 basis points alongside advisor-led models — wirehouses at approximately 59 basis points and regionals & independent broker-dealers at approximately 87 basis points — in a single chart on a common basis. This comparison rests on Schwab's own figures rather than figures independently reported on a consistent basis by the advisor-led firms: Morgan Stanley, Edward Jones, and Merrill do not report a comparable revenue-yield-on-client-assets figure in the evidence provided, so the comparison cannot be independently reproduced across firms. Raymond James's Chair and CEO separately stated (on the Q4 2024 earnings call) that in the RIA and Custody Services division the firm earns an asset fee and that, compared with pure RIAs, Raymond James's net basis points on client assets are lower, with part of the difference attributable to the different service model and the absence of the same supervision and compliance requirements — a qualitative statement rather than a reported yield figure.

items.text: Deloitte states that for clients, faster responses, more tailored insights, and more proactive outreach should become minimum standards as agentic AI reshapes how advice is created, packaged, and delivered.
items.quote: For clients, the bar should rise quickly. Faster responses, more tailored insights, and more proactive outreach should become minimum standards.

items.text: Deloitte states advisers spend nearly 70% of their time on behind-the-scenes work and that AI has the potential to flip that toward more time building client relationships.
items.quote: Advisers spend nearly 70% of their time on behind-the-scenes work, leaving just 30% for where they add the most value—building client relationships. Artificial intelligence, especially agentic execution, has the potential to flip that equation.

items.text: Capgemini states AI-powered next-best actions aligned to client goals enable personalized experiences at scale for high-net-worth clients.
items.quote: AI-powered next-best actions aligned to client goals enable personalized experiences at scale, demonstrate value beyond investment returns, and build the trust that keeps high-net-worth clients engaged.

items.text: Capgemini states augmented intelligence strengthens human capability by providing better information, faster insights, and broader context, enabling better decisions and more meaningful client engagement.
items.quote: Augmentation strengthens human capability by providing better information, faster insights, and broader context, enabling better decisions and more meaningful client engagement.

items.text: Wealthtender states one-third of prospects prefer online meetings exclusively, creating opportunity for practice growth beyond geographic limitations through virtual service models.
items.quote: One-third of prospects don't care about advisor location, preferring online meetings exclusively.

items.text: Wealthtender anticipates continued growth in AI tool usage for advisor searches, increasing expectation for faster response times and digital-first communications, and further acceptance of virtual advisor relationships regardless of geographic location.
items.quote: 1) Continued growth in AI tool usage for advisor searches, 2) Increasing expectation for faster response times and digital-first communications... 5) Further acceptance of virtual advisor relationships regardless of geographic location.

items.text: Schwab states 77% of U.S. investors use AI today and 90%+ prefer human involvement alongside AI, and that AI is creating more personalized client experiences and greater productivity at scale.
items.quote: 77% of U.S. Investors Use AI Today 90%+ Prefer Human Involvement Alongside AI... AI is amplifying our platform advantage, creating more personalized client experiences & greater productivity at scale.

items.text: Accenture reports 96% of surveyed wealth professionals say AI is transforming how advice is created for, delivered to, and consumed by clients today.
items.quote: say AI is transforming how advice to, and consumed by clients 96% is created for, today.

items.quote: Introduced Charley, a new AI-powered assistant that provides U.S. retail clients with conversational access to Schwab's tools and insights

items.text: Edward Jones states the financial services industry provides enhanced digital experiences for clients, including artificial intelligence technologies and lower-cost computer-based robo-advice.
items.quote: an increasing number of firms of all sizes providing enhanced digital experiences for clients, including the utilization of artificial intelligence technologies and lower cost, computer-based "robo-advice."

items.text: Bank of America Private Bank states it uses AI to support advisor capacity and deepen client relationships, and that 93% of Private Bank clients were digitally active in 2025.
items.quote: Bank of America Private Bank uses AI to support advisor capacity, deepen client relationships, and help teams find information faster and more efficiently. In 2025, ninety three percent 93% of Private Bank clients were digitally active

items.text: Merrill launched Tax Efficient Transition Service and Dollar Cost Averaging Service that combine automation with professional portfolio oversight to help clients simplify asset transitions and cash deployment.
items.quote: new services that combine automation with professional portfolio oversight to help clients simplify asset transitions and cash deployment into managed or custom managed investment strategies

items.text: Schwab introduced Portfolio Insights, a generative AI-powered capability that helps investors understand portfolio performance through narrative snapshots and recaps.
items.quote: Portfolio Insights (Insights) is a generative artificial intelligence feature designed to provide: (1) a narrative snapshot of a client's Portfolio's Day Change performance

items.text: Capgemini's World Wealth Report states that advances in artificial intelligence are enabling augmented intelligence - technology that enhances rather than replaces human judgment - and that wealth management is shifting from product-centric distribution to empathy-led advice extending beyond portfolios into clients' lives.
items.quote: Advances in artificial intelligence are accelerating this shift, enabling firms to process vast amounts of data, uncover deeper insights, and respond to client needs with greater speed and precision. At the heart of this shift is augmented intelligence - not technology that replaces human judgment, but technology that enhances it... wealth management is shifting from product-centric distribution to empathy-led advice - advice that extends beyond portfolios into the broader context of clients' lives.

items.text: Capgemini describes a target-state implementation with an adaptive AI engine that dynamically tailors content depth, tone, and engagement pathways based on investor personas and life-event context, plus a Personal Wealth Coach that equips relationship managers with governed AI copilots and personalized nudges.
items.quote: An Adaptive Experience AI Engine with Knowledge Management as a Service (KMaaS) dynamically tailors content depth, tone, and engagement pathways based on investor personas and life-event context... a Personal Wealth Coach and Intelligence Marketplace equips RMs with governed AI copilots, personalized nudges, and meeting intelligence

items.text: Capgemini's report says the wealth management landscape is shifting from selling products to offering personalized, empathetic advice, and in its "Later" horizon foresees autonomous portfolio delivery and AI-enabled estate and tax planning embedded in client journeys.
items.quote: The wealth management landscape is shifting from selling products to offering personalized, empathetic advice... In the Later horizon, the operating model reaches full maturity: autonomous portfolio delivery, AI-enabled estate and tax planning embedded in client journeys

items.text: Capgemini describes SCB's MyWealth advisor integrating generative AI alongside the advisory workflow to draft client communications and reduce the time needed to prepare for each client conversation, enhancing quality of advice.
items.quote: SCB has also integrated generative AI capabilities alongside the advisory workflow to support RM productivity, including drafting of client communications... The solutions reduced the time needed to prepare for each client conversation.

items.text: Raymond James' CEO says the firm wants to use AI to help its financial professionals and advisors better serve their clients and empower advisors, whereas many competitors use AI to go direct to clients.
items.quote: we're really wanting to use AI to help our financial professionals and our financial advisors better serve their clients, where many of our competitors have used technology and are planning on using AI to essentially try to get around their financial advisors to go direct to their clients... Our goal is to use AI to better empower our advisors and financial professionals so they could provide even better service to their clients.

items.text: Bank of America's CFO says the trends will be more technology, more intimacy with customers, more agentic (versus prompt) AI, and more built into the process rather than delivered by teammates.
items.quote: the trends will be more technology, more intimacy with the customers more agentic versus prompt more built into the process rather than have it be delivered by teammates doing something, it's part of the process

This comparison cannot be made validly on a single common basis. The firms report different quantities with no shared metric or definition: Bank of America cites use-case counts and a virtual assistant (Erica, over 58 million interactions per month; more than 300 AI/ML use cases approved and 114 live generative AI use cases); Schwab cites use-case counts, developer-productivity percentages, and client-facing positioning (40 then more than 220 use cases, ~25% developer productivity increase, and claims it is already an AI-enabled company and #1 in the space); Raymond James cites dollar technology spend (approximately $1 billion to $1.1 billion), Raimond user counts (6,500 unique users, 99.5% satisfaction), and an AI framework; Morgan Stanley cites use cases (DevGen AI, Parable, LeadIQ) and a CEO statement calling AI absolutely the top priority for the firm and existentially important, having been overweighted and now double overweight to AI in wealth; and Edward Jones cites third-party partnerships (Aboon, Quicken). Because these are different definitions, units, scopes and periods (use-case counts, dollar spend, productivity percentages, subjective positioning statements), the firms are not comparable on a like-for-like basis, so no single firm can be ranked as making the most extensive or strongest claims from this evidence alone.

a1.all.label: fact

items.text: McKinsey's PriceMetrix data show that after a period of fee compression for advisory relationships from 2013 to 2018, advisory fee rates have stabilized; fee rates for $1.0 million to $1.5 million advisory relationships have stayed at an average of approximately 104 basis points since 2019.
items.quote: After a period of fee compression for advisory relationships from 2013 to 2018, fee rates have stabilized, according to PriceMetrix by McKinsey. For example, fee rates for $1.0 million to $1.5 million advisory relationships have stayed at an average of approximately 104 basis points since 2019.
items.scope: advisory relationships of $1.0 million to $1.5 million

items.text: McKinsey believes fee pressure will be uneven, manifesting as demands for transparency and unbundled pricing rather than a blanket reduction in basis points.
items.quote: We believe fee pressure will be uneven, manifesting as demands for transparency and unbundled pricing rather than a blanket reduction in basis points.

items.text: Edward Jones states there has been ongoing fee compression across the mutual fund industry in recent years, and that continued changes in industry fee structures and further compression of management or distribution fees could materially impact margins.
items.quote: driven in large part by the ongoing fee compression that has occurred across the mutual fund industry in recent years... Continued changes in industry fee structures, further compression of management or distribution fees, regulatory reform or other changes to the Partnership's relationship with mutual fund or insurance companies could have a material adverse effect

items.text: Raymond James states that regulatory requirements have resulted in greater price transparency in fixed income and equity markets, leading to price competition and decreased trading margins, and that price competition and pricing pressures will continue.
items.quote: In fixed income and equity markets, regulatory requirements have resulted in greater price transparency, leading to price competition and decreased trading margins.

items.text: Cerulli reports that for the past decade, financial firms have shifted their compensation models from largely commission-based to an asset-related fee structure.
items.quote: For the past decade, financial firms have shifted their compensation models from largely commission-based to an asset-related fee structure.

items.text: Cerulli attributes the rise in investors' willingness to pay for advice in part to continued fee compression across both advisors and product fees.
items.quote: This 30-percentage-point increase can be attributed in part to greater accessibility of financial advice, continued fee compression across both advisors and product fees, and the proliferation of fiduciary advice

items.text: Deloitte notes that while lower cost-to-serve can expand margins for firms that maintain pricing, competitive pressure may compress fees as planning outputs become easier to compare.
items.quote: Lower cost-to-serve can expand margins for firms that execute and maintain pricing. At the same time, competitive pressure may compress fees as planning outputs become easier to compare.

items.text: Industry observers state that new platform fees appearing at major distributors are directly or indirectly traceable to the zeroing out of commissions in the brokerage industry.
items.quote: A number of sources made the point that all these platform tolls showing up at the giant distributors are directly or indirectly traceable to the zeroing out of commissions in the brokerage industry.

items.text: Schwab's CFO states that investors' preferences are for lower explicit fees without sacrificing product access, convenience or service.
items.quote: Our model is informed by investors' preferences for lower explicit fees without sacrificing product access, convenience or service.

items.text: McKinsey reports industry leaders are worried whether the rapid commoditization of technical expertise will erode the barriers to entry that have historically protected high-margin advisory fees.
items.quote: Industry leaders are worried whether the rapid commoditization of technical expertise will erode the barriers to entry that have historically protected high-margin advisory fees.

items.text: Raymond James notes that the market environment has resulted in a shift to passive investment products, which generate lower fees than actively managed products.
items.quote: the market environment in recent years has resulted in a shift to passive investment products, which generate lower fees than actively managed products.

items.text: A survey found that 73% of participants consider transparency in fees and services crucial for establishing an advisor's credibility, making fee transparency the top trust factor.
items.quote: Nearly three-quarters (73%) of survey participants said transparency in fees and services is crucial for establishing an advisor's credibility.

items.text: Industry commentary notes that the SEC's sustained focus on cash sweep disclosures, combined with litigation over allegedly low client yields, keeps cash sweep transparency and pricing a live issue.
items.quote: The SEC's sustained focus on sweep disclosures, combined with a wave of litigation against major firms over allegedly low client yields, means that the question of who benefits from rising rates on uninvested cash is unlikely to fade from client conversations any time soon.

items.text: Schwab states that it periodically adjusts pricing on deposits, loans, advisory fees, fund expense ratios, trade commissions and other pricing and incentives, and that increased price competition across the industry—such as reduced commissions, higher deposit rates, reduced mutual fund or ETF expense ratios, or increased use of incentives—could affect results.
items.quote: We continually monitor our pricing in relation to competitors and periodically adjust interest rates on deposits and loans, fees for advisory services, expense ratios on mutual funds and ETFs, trade commission rates, and other pricing and incentives to sustain our competitive position. Increased price competition from other financial services firms to attract clients, such as reduced commissions, higher deposit rates, reduced mutual fund or ETF expense ratios, or the increased use of incentives, could impact our results of operations and financial condition.

items.text: Fidelity introduced ETF platform and revenue-sharing fees in March 2024 (including a $100 ticket charge on trades of funds that refused to pay shelf-space fees), and major wirehouses including UBS and Wells Fargo introduced data fees in the mid-2010s and 2020 respectively; the widespread adoption of data fees to offset declining transaction revenue was first predicted in 2019 when Charles Schwab began charging for data it had previously provided free.
items.quote: Fidelity introduced ETF platform and revenue sharing fees in March 2024 – including a $100 ticket charge on trades of funds that refused to pay shelf-space fees – and major wires, including UBS and Wells Fargo introduced data fees in the mid-2010s, and 2020, respectively. Pirker first predicted the widespread adoption of data fees to offset declining transaction revenue in 2019, when Charles Schwab & Co. began charging for data it had historically provided for free.

items.text: Research notes that AI challenges assumptions underpinning wealth management economics and that, as the marginal cost of generating tax analysis, scenario modeling, portfolio commentary and meeting documentation collapses, fee durability requires rigorous reexamination.
items.quote: If the marginal cost of generating tax analysis, scenario modeling, portfolio commentary, and meeting documentation collapses, then operating leverage, advisor capacity, and fee durability require rigorous reexamination.

items.text: Schwab noted a slight offset in its other revenue line due to the SEC's decision to lower exchange processing fees to zero beginning in mid-May, a rate change it described as P&L neutral.
items.quote: Note that there was a slight offset in this other line due to the SEC's decision to lower exchange processing fees to zero beginning in mid-May. Of course, this rate change is P&L neutral, as there is a corresponding decrease in the other expense line as well.

items.text: Schwab's 10-Q lists "SEC transaction fee increases" among forward-looking statements concerning results of operations, indicating expected increases in transaction fees.
items.quote: SEC transaction fee increases (see Results of Operations in Part I - Item 2);

A survey of people hiring financial advisors (published August 13, 2025) found that just over 38% of people consider a lack of transparency about fees or commissions a major red flag, and that if an advisor cannot clearly explain their pricing structure it undermines trust.

Schwab's CEO stated on the 2025 second-quarter earnings call (quarter ended June 30, 2025) that for 50 years Schwab has innovated from a standpoint of what is right for clients, alongside regulators, in a way that creates transparency, low-cost, effective markets.

Morgan Stanley states (Form ADV, published November 4, 2026) that under DOL regulations under ERISA Section 408(b)(2), it must provide information on its services and compensation to fiduciaries to assess the reasonableness of compensation. Why it might matter: Bank of America separately notes increasing pressure to provide products and services on more attractive terms, including lower fees, lower cost investment strategies and higher interest rates on deposits.

A trade report (published November 4, 2026) states that under the SEC's Marketing Rule (Rule 206(4)-1), financial firms are legally exposed if they promote third-party ratings or badges that cannot be verified as completely impartial. Why it might matter: the report states such awards posed a reputational risk for Morgan Stanley and potentially multi-million dollar SEC penalties.

The SEC entered a settlement order with Morgan Stanley Wealth Management finding that from 2009 through 2015 it inadvertently charged advisory fees in excess of what had been disclosed to and agreed to by its legacy clients (Form ADV, published November 4, 2026). Why it might matter: the settlement also found that from 2002 to 2016 the firm's predecessors charged fees in excess of what was disclosed to and agreed to by their clients.

Merrill Lynch states (Form ADV, published October 30, 2026) that under DOL regulations under ERISA Section 408(b)(2), it must provide compensation information to fiduciaries and plan sponsors of retirement accounts to assess the reasonableness of compensation. Why it might matter: the firm states this information is provided at the outset of the relationship through Retirement Account Addendum/408(b)(2) fee disclosures.

Merrill Lynch states (Form ADV, published October 30, 2026) the SEC issued an administrative order finding its wrap fee program disclosures contained a material misstatement because a production credit fee was charged but not disclosed alongside the disclosed currency mark-up. Why it might matter: the SEC order also found a failure to adopt and implement written policies and procedures reasonably designed to address the relevant fee disclosure.

A trade report (published October 26, 2026) states large team departures may now be structural given the attractive economics in RIA ownership, prompting Ameriprise to respond with reductions to platform fees, alongside cash retention bonuses, to retain advisors. Why it might matter: the report notes stronger recruiting and retention from the wirehouses has also slowed breakaways to independent broker-dealers.

State securities regulators led by NASAA announced a combined $4.4 million settlement with Wells Fargo and Merrill Lynch over charges of unreasonable commissions on small-dollar retail equity transactions, with restitution ordered on over 256,000 transactions over a five-year period (trade report published October 16, 2026). Why it might matter: the investigation was led by Massachusetts and joined by regulators in multiple other states.

Schwab states (Form ADV, published October 15, 2026) that the SEC found it made false and misleading statements in Form ADV Part 2A brochures about cash allocations in Schwab Intelligent Portfolios accounts, including its conflict of interest in setting cash allocations. Why it might matter: Schwab states the SEC found the firm and its former affiliate violated provisions of the Advisers Act from March 2015 through November 2018.

Industry commentary (trade report published September 30, 2026) notes the SEC is sustaining its focus on cash sweep disclosures, and a wave of litigation against major firms over allegedly low client yields keeps the question of who benefits from rising rates on uninvested cash alive in client conversations. Why it might matter: the report states advisors should be prepared to explain how their custodian's sweep structure works and how it may shift with the rate environment.

Industry observers state that the platform tolls (data and support fees) appearing at large distributors are directly or indirectly traceable to the zeroing out of commissions in the brokerage industry, as revenue replacement must come from somewhere if loads are no longer charged on funds (trade report published September 29, 2026). Why it might matter: observers note distributors have real costs to distributing, though Merrill cannot lean as heavily on that argument for its full-service brokers.

Raymond James states (10-Q, period ended June 30, 2026) that beginning August 2024 the SEC's Division of Enforcement requested information regarding its cash sweep program practices for advisory clients and has reportedly conducted similar reviews at other institutions. Why it might matter: the firm states it has been cooperating with this inquiry.

Capgemini (published June 3, 2026) projects the robo advisory market will grow at a 44.1% CAGR for AUM between 2024 and 2030, and digital-first clients prefer robo-advisory platforms that deliver seamless, low-cost, self-directed experiences. Why it might matter: Capgemini notes specialized providers with differentiated value propositions are scaling faster, while mid-tier HNWIs increasingly rely on RIAs providing flexible, fiduciary advice.

Schwab states (2026 first-quarter earnings call, quarter ended March 31, 2026) that its model is informed by investors' preferences for lower explicit fees without sacrificing product access, convenience, or service. Why it might matter: Schwab states that if those preferences change in the future, it has flexibility to continue supporting investors and RIAs while still delivering strong returns.

Schwab CEO Rick Wurster stated (2026 first-quarter earnings call, quarter ended March 31, 2026) that, according to research, more than half of the firm's clients are willing to pay for AI financial tools, which over time will create opportunities for new fee-based offers. Why it might matter: the CEO stated AI is already driving scale and efficiency by helping drive productivity across the firm.

McKinsey (published April 8, 2026) anticipates that fee pressure in wealth management will be uneven, manifesting as client demands for transparency and unbundled pricing rather than a blanket reduction in basis points. Why it might matter: McKinsey notes fee rates for relationships over $1 million have remained remarkably steady at about 104 basis points since 2019 even as digital tools proliferated.

Edward Jones states in its 2025 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025) that it is subject to the SEC rule requiring delivery of a Form CRS Relationship Summary informing clients of fees, costs, conflicts of interest, and disciplinary history. Why it might matter: Edward Jones notes the SEC has also issued guidance clarifying the fiduciary standard applicable to advisory relationships.

Edward Jones states in its 2025 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025) that it competes with major competitor brokerage firms that offer zero commissions for purchases and sales of stocks, ETFs and other brokerage products, and with firms offering lower cost, computer-based robo-advice. Why it might matter: Edward Jones notes clients can transfer their business to competing organizations at any time, and the firm also faces competition from fintech companies.

Schwab states in its 2025 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025) that the wealth management industry is highly competitive and characterized by aggressive price competition. Why it might matter: Edward Jones separately notes there has been ongoing fee compression across the mutual fund industry in recent years.

Schwab states in its 2025 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025) that regulations governing broker-dealers cover, among other things, fee arrangements, order flow revenue, disclosure to clients, and fiduciary duties. Why it might matter: Schwab states the principal purpose of regulating these entities is the protection of clients and securities markets.

Schwab states in its 2025 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025) that the SEC withdrew the proposed Order Competition Rule and Regulation Best Execution in June 2025, which the company had been evaluating. Why it might matter: Schwab also states the FDIC withdrew certain notices of proposed rulemaking on March 3, 2025.

Bank of America states in its 2025 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025) that increasing pressure to provide products and services on more attractive terms, including lower fees, lower cost investment strategies and higher interest rates on deposits, may impact its ability to effectively compete. Why it might matter: the bank states it may be disadvantaged by its size, the jurisdictions in which it operates, or more stringent regulatory requirements applicable to it than to nonbank competitors.

Bank of America states in its 2025 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025) that emerging technologies and the growth of e-commerce have made it easier for non-depository institutions to offer electronic securities trading with low or no fees and commissions, and that increased competition may reduce fee-based revenue through pricing pressure. Why it might matter: the bank notes the growth of and mergers among traditional financial services companies have also increased competition.

Schwab states in its 2025 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025) that increased price competition from other financial services firms to attract clients, such as reduced commissions, higher deposit rates, reduced mutual fund or ETF expense ratios, or the increased use of incentives, could impact its results. Why it might matter: Schwab states it continually monitors its pricing in relation to competitors and periodically adjusts fees and incentives to sustain its competitive position.

Morgan Stanley states in its 2025 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025) that its broker-dealers are subject to the SEC's Regulation Best Interest, which requires them to act in the best interest of retail customers when making a recommendation without placing their own interests ahead of the customer's. Why it might matter: Morgan Stanley notes its investment advisory client relationships are also subject to fiduciary obligations and that the SEC and other supervisory bodies have broad administrative powers to address non-compliance.

Morgan Stanley states in its 2025 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025) that it has experienced pricing pressures as competitors seek to obtain market share by reducing prices and fees, paying higher interest rates on deposits, eliminating commissions or other fees, or otherwise providing more favorable terms of business. Why it might matter: the firm states certain competitors may be subject to less stringent legal and regulatory regimes, putting it at a competitive disadvantage.

Morgan Stanley states in its 2025 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025) that it continues to experience price competition in its Institutional Securities business segment as the ability to execute trades electronically on automated platforms will likely continue the pressure on revenues. Why it might matter: the firm states the introduction of new technologies, including generative AI and tokenization, will likely continue the pressure on its revenues.

Raymond James states in its 2025 10-K (period ended September 30, 2025) that Regulation Best Interest and Form CRS required it to implement additional client disclosures and education, and that various states have proposed or adopted differing conduct standards. Why it might matter: various states have also proposed or adopted laws and regulations seeking to impose new standards of conduct on broker-dealers.

Raymond James states in its 2025 10-K (period ended September 30, 2025) that the UK FCA Consumer Duty, effective July 31, 2023, requires firms to deliver good outcomes for retail customers with respect to price and value, among other things. Why it might matter: in April 2024 the Department of Labor issued a final rule significantly expanding the definition of investment advice fiduciary under ERISA.

Raymond James states in its 2025 10-K (period ended September 30, 2025) that regulatory requirements have resulted in greater price transparency, leading to price competition and decreased trading margins, and that trading margins have been further compressed by the shift from high- to low-touch services, while some competitors seek to obtain market share by reducing fees, commissions, or margins. Why it might matter: the firm states it periodically may need to adjust its fees, commissions, margins, or interest rates on deposits to remain competitive.

Fidelity's 2025 Investor Insights Study (published October 9, 2025) finds that wealthy next-generation (Gen X, Y, and Z) high-net-worth households seek transparency in advisor compensation, along with broader life guidance and emerging investment products. Why it might matter: the study states advisors must adapt to these shifting dynamics to effectively serve this generation's distinctive demands.

A Wealthtender publication (published August 13, 2025) states the SEC established a rule in 2021 requiring advisors who display only a handful of self-picked testimonials on their website to also link to an online location where all of their reviews can be read. Why it might matter: the source advises that testimonials on an advisor's website are useful only if accompanied by a link to a location where all reviews can be read.

Survey data (published August 13, 2025) shows 48% of participants consider pricing and overall anticipated costs among the top three factors in choosing an advisor, indicating transparent, reasonable pricing is a dealmaker rather than simply being cheapest. Why it might matter: the source states transparent, reasonable pricing gives clients peace of mind and helps them budget.

A consumer survey (published August 13, 2025) found nearly three-quarters (73%) of survey participants said transparency in fees and services is crucial for establishing an advisor's credibility, making fee transparency the top trust factor driving transparency. Why it might matter: the source identifies clear, upfront communication about costs as the most important factor for building trust.

Wealthtender's study (published August 13, 2025) reports pricing and overall anticipated cost is the top factor (48%) in final advisor selection, exerting competitive pressure on pricing. Why it might matter: the source cautions this does not mean choosing the cheapest option is best, and advises focusing on value for the fees paid.

The Wealthtender advisor search study (conducted July 2025, published August 13, 2025) found that fee transparency is a 73% priority for consumers researching financial advisors. Why it might matter: the study advises advisors to ensure their pricing is clearly communicated across all marketing materials.

Wealthtender (published August 13, 2025) reports consumers researching advisors prioritize fee transparency, professional credentials, and positive client reviews. Why it might matter: the source also advises consumers to focus on advisors who specialize in their particular needs and life stage.

Schwab's 2025 second-quarter earnings call (quarter ended June 30, 2025) references the mid-May reduction of the SEC 31 fee rate. Why it might matter: Schwab separately noted a slight offset in its other revenue line due to the SEC's decision to lower exchange processing fees to zero beginning in mid-May, a rate change it described as P&L neutral.

Vanguard (published June 4, 2025) found that for digital advice, the key attributes valued by clients include the need for transparency (visibility of portfolio changes) and an awareness of fees. Why it might matter: Vanguard contrasts this with human advice, where value is mostly derived from a client's relationship with their financial advisor.

According to Cerulli (published May 28, 2025), fee-based planning is the most preferred form of compensating an advisor among affluent investors, preferred by 36%, although some investors still prefer commission-based or no-fee services. Why it might matter: Cerulli notes this shift improves the standing of financial firms as fiduciaries since compensation is tied to portfolio performance rather than selling particular products.

According to McKinsey (published February 10, 2025), increasing demand for human advice is one of the factors behind stable to slightly increasing advisory fee rates across delivery models. Why it might matter: McKinsey notes that among investors with more than $1 million in investable assets, the share willing to pay a premium of 100 basis points or more grew by 50 percent.

The comparison of which firms lead or lag on fee structure changes and transparency cannot be validly made on this evidence as a whole, because the items are not on a same basis: they cover different fee types (data/shelf fees, trading commissions and margins, advisory fees), different scopes, and different time periods, with no shared metric against which firms are ranked. Within the narrower slice of data/shelf fees, trade-press reporting (published September 29, 2026) states Merrill Lynch is among the last major wealth management firms to maximize data/shelf fees, while Charles Schwab began charging for advisor data in 2019 earlier than peers, and Merrill notes its new data analytics fee scale is comparable to peers, with Wells Fargo levying up to $1.15 million, UBS between $150,000 and $300,000, and Morgan Stanley between $25,000 and $500,000; but these bear only on data/shelf fees, not on fee structure changes and transparency overall.

a6.EDJ.label: fact

items.text: Edward Jones states its strategic ambition is to help tens of millions of investors achieve financial fulfillment through personalized, comprehensive planning and trusted advice, and that to do so it aspires to continue investing in technology to scale financial planning, to anticipate clients' needs with the right offering at the right time now and for generations to come, and to attract and serve new client segments.
items.quote: The Partnership's strategic ambition is to help tens of millions of investors achieve financial fulfillment through personalized, comprehensive planning and trusted advice. To do this, the Partnership aspires to: • Continue investing in technology to scale our ability to provide financial planning to our clients • Anticipate clients' needs with the right offering at the right time, now and for generations to come • Attract and serve new client segments

items.text: Edward Jones states that among its initiatives to target new clients is a new digital platform focused on attracting and retaining Next Generation investors.
items.quote: These initiatives also include targeting new clients: High Net Worth, focused on attracting and serving high net worth clients through expanded advice, planning, products and services across multiple service models; Workplace, which connects local business owners and their employees with financial solutions through their workplace; and a new digital platform, focused on attracting and retaining Next Generation investors.

items.text: Edward Jones states it seeks to address its strategic risks, most notably competition for clients and personnel in light of the evolving financial services industry and generational wealth transfer, changing client demographics, preferences and values, through its initiatives to deliver enhanced value and impact for millions of current and potential clients, and is continuing to make significant investments to attract and retain qualified talent.
items.quote: The Partnership seeks to address its strategic risks, most notably competition for clients and personnel in light of the evolving financial services industry and generational wealth transfer, changing client demographics, preferences and values, technology, artificial intelligence, and regulatory changes, through its initiatives to deliver enhanced value and impact for millions of current and potential clients, colleagues and communities.

a6.EDJ.reason: The passages state Edward Jones's strategy and priorities for attracting new client segments including Next Generation investors, without quantifying specific under-40 figures.

items.text: Cerulli states that younger investors are more comfortable directing their own investing through online brokerages, so financial advisors looking to connect with these prospective clients must be able to articulate benefits outside of the investing realm, such as financial planning, lending, and tax services.
items.quote: Younger investors typically are more comfortable directing their own investing through online brokerages (e.g., E*TRADE, Fidelity), meaning financial advisors looking to connect with these prospective clients must be able to articulate benefits outside of the investing realm, such as financial planning, lending, and tax services.

items.text: Cerulli states that while older investors tend to be more advisor-reliant, younger investors prefer to retain a greater degree of control over at least part of their investing lives.
items.quote: While older investors tend to be more advisor-reliant, younger investors prefer to retain a greater degree of control of at least part of their investing lives.

items.text: Bank of America Private Bank's 2026 Study of Wealthy Americans finds that 65% of young investors still prefer to receive investment advice from a human advisor, even as 87% are comfortable with advisors using AI.
items.quote: eighty seven percent 87% are comfortable with advisors using AI to help manage portfolios, yet sixty five percent 65% still prefer to receive investment advice from a human advisor.
items.unit: of young investors preferring human advice

items.text: Schwab states that younger clients turn to the firm because it meets them in the channels where they seek investing information, noting they learn about finances primarily through social media and family.
items.quote: One of the reasons they're turning to Schwab is because we're meeting them in the channels where they turn for information about investing. We know they learn about finances primarily through social media and family.

items.text: Schwab states that younger investors' top online resource is YouTube, where Schwab is the number one financial services firm by followers.
items.quote: Their top online resource is YouTube, and we're the number one financial services firm on YouTube by followers.

items.text: The CFPB finds that Millennials and Gen Z are more likely than older adults to act on financial information without further validation, especially from online sources, and those aged 25-45 are more trusting of financial information from generative AI tools and social media than older Americans.
items.quote: Millennials and Gen Z are more likely than older adults to act on financial information they encounter without further validation, especially from online sources. Those aged 25-45 are more trusting than older Americans aged 46-64 of the financial information obtained from generative AI tools (44% vs. 26%) and social media (44% vs. 24%).

items.text: Bank of America Private Bank's 2026 Study of Wealthy Americans reports that 65% of young investors still prefer to receive investment advice from a human advisor, even as they embrace AI.
items.quote: sixty five percent 65% still prefer to receive investment advice from a human advisor.
items.scope: young investors (Gen Z and Millennials, ages 21 to 45)

a1.all.reason: Multiple passages state factors that drive clients under 40 in choosing or engaging with financial advisors (control preference, human advisor preference, channels/social media, trust in online sources), so these are facts.

a2.all.label: fact

items.text: In the Wealthtender advisor-search survey, the top resources consumers plan to use to find a financial advisor are referrals from friends or family (62.00%), search engines (49.80%), financial institutions such as a bank or credit union (49.00%), and referrals from professionals such as an accountant or attorney (49.20%).
items.quote: Which resource(s) do you plan to find a financial advisor? ... Referrals from friends or family 62.00% ... Search engines (e.g., Google, Bing) 49.80% ... Financial institution (e.g., bank, credit union) 49.00% ... Referrals from professionals (e.g., accountant, attorney) 49.20%

items.text: In the Wealthtender survey, 25% of people plan to use AI tools such as ChatGPT or Gemini to start their advisor search, about one-third (32%) will use online advisor directories like Wealthtender, and about 22% will be influenced by social media platforms like LinkedIn, Reddit, and Facebook.
items.quote: 25% of people plan to use ChatGPT, Gemini or other AI-powered tools to start their advisor search ... Online advisor directories like Wealthtender will be used as a starting point by about one-third of consumers (32%), while social media platforms like LinkedIn, Reddit, and Facebook influence about 22% of people.

items.text: In the Wealthtender survey, 96% of people said they would still research an advisor even if that advisor came highly recommended.
items.quote: 96% of people in our survey said they would still research an advisor even if that advisor came highly recommended.

items.text: The CFPB reports that younger Americans are far more likely to embrace social media, podcasts, and generative AI to meet their financial information needs.
items.quote: Younger Americans are far more likely to embrace social media, podcasts and generative AI to meet their financial information needs.

items.text: Schwab's CEO states that Gen Z clients (investors between the ages of 13 and 28) learn about finances primarily through social media and family.
items.quote: We know they learn about finances primarily through social media and family.

items.text: Schwab's CEO states that younger investors' top online resource is YouTube.
items.quote: Their top online resource is YouTube, and we're the number one financial services firm on YouTube by followers.

items.text: FINRA research reports that 36 percent of social media users and 41 percent of finfluencer followers check the background, registration, or license of a financial professional with a state or federal regulator, versus 14 percent of non-users and 13 percent of non-followers.
items.quote: 36 percent of social media users and 41 percent of finfluencer followers report checking the background, registration or license of a financial professional with a state or federal regulator, a much higher proportion than for non-users (14 percent) or non-followers (13 percent).

items.text: According to CFPB research, Millennials and Gen Z are more likely than older adults to act on financial information they encounter without further validation, especially from online sources.
items.quote: Millennials and Gen Z are more likely than older adults to act on financial information they encounter without further validation, especially from online sources.

a2.all.reason: The CFPB research passage gives age-specific findings on the online sources (generative AI tools, social media) that Millennials/Gen Z and those aged 25-45 trust for financial information, which is the closest evidence for channels/sources used by clients under 40.

a3.all.label: fact

items.text: In the 2025 Wealthtender Voice of the Client study, the top financial goals or needs respondents would seek a financial advisor's help with are retirement planning and income strategies (63%), investment management and portfolio growth (53%), tax planning and optimization (29%), estate planning and wealth transfer (26%), debt management and reduction (16%), budgeting and cash flow management (14%), saving for a major purchase such as a home or business (13%), insurance needs and risk management (11%), and saving for children's education (10%).
items.quote: What are your top 2-3 most important financial goals or needs that you would seek a financial advisor's help with?... Retirement planning and income strategies 63... Investment management and portfolio growth 53... Debt management and reduction 16... Budgeting and cash flow management 14... Tax planning and optimization 29... Estate planning and wealth transfer 26... Saving for a major purchase (e.g., home, business) 13... Saving for children's education 10... Insurance needs and risk management 11

items.text: For the next generation, experience and expertise sit at the top of the wish list when choosing a wealth manager (79%), and more than half (56%) want advisors who can build trusted relationships across generations, while 41% value an advisor's ability to fully understand the next generation's needs.
items.quote: When choosing a wealth manager, experience and expertise sit at the top of the next generation's wish list (79%)... More than half (56%) want advisors who can build trusted relationships across generations... their ability to fully understand the next generation's needs (41%).

items.text: Cerulli notes that Millennials have contended with heightened student debt and economic upheaval, and recent higher mortgage rates have put the goal of home ownership further out of reach; as a result, some Millennials have delayed traditional life milestones such as getting married, buying a home, and having children.
items.quote: They also have contended with heightened student debt and the economic upheaval of the pandemic... recent higher mortgage rates have put the goal of home ownership further out of reach for some. As a result, some Millennials have delayed traditional milestones such as getting married, buying a home, and having children.

items.text: By generation, the top three most important investment goals for Millennials are to grow wealth over time, plan for comfortable or early retirement, and achieve financial independence.
items.quote: Top Three Most Important Investment Goals by Generation... Millennials (born early 1980s-mid-1990s)... Grow wealth over time... Plan for comfortable or early retirement... Financial independence

items.text: Competing financial priorities materially constrain retirement saving for a much larger share of younger generations: approximately 30% of working Baby Boomers report this, rising to more than 50% for Gen X, exceeding 75% for Millennials, and remaining above 70% for Gen Z.
items.quote: approximately 30% of working Baby Boomers report that competing priorities materially constrain retirement saving; this share rises to more than 50% for Gen X, exceeds 75% for Millennials, and remains above 70% for Gen Z.

items.text: The competing priorities affecting respondents' ability to save for retirement include credit card debt, paying down existing loans (student loans, etc.), saving for college, caring for and financially supporting family members, time out of the workforce (e.g., child or elder care), financial hardship (home repairs, etc.), and too many monthly financial expenses; younger generations (Gen X, Millennials, Gen Z) report a significantly higher impact from these challenges than Baby Boomers, with Millennials the most impacted.
items.quote: a distinct generational divide persists in how these competing priorities affect retirement savings. Younger generations, specifically Generation X, Millennials, and Generation Z, consistently report a significantly higher impact from these challenges compared to Baby Boomers. Millennials, for instance, are noted as being the most impacted.

Bank of America Private Bank's 2026 Study of Wealthy Americans (published 2026-06-17) finds that 65% of young investors still prefer to receive investment advice from a human advisor, even as 87% are comfortable with advisors using AI.

Schwab (period ended 2025-09-30) states that younger clients turn to the firm because it meets them in the channels where they seek investing information, noting they learn about finances primarily through social media and family.
Schwab (period ended 2025-09-30) states that younger investors' top online resource is YouTube, where Schwab is the number one financial services firm by followers.

In the Wealthtender advisor-search survey (published 2025-08-13), the top resources consumers plan to use to find a financial advisor are referrals from friends or family (62.00%), search engines (49.80%), financial institutions such as a bank or credit union (49.00%), and referrals from professionals such as an accountant or attorney (49.20%).

In the Wealthtender survey, 25% of people plan to use AI tools such as ChatGPT or Gemini to start their advisor search, about one-third (32%) will use online advisor directories like Wealthtender, and about 22% will be influenced by social media platforms like LinkedIn, Reddit, and Facebook.
In the Wealthtender survey, 96% of people said they would still research an advisor even if that advisor came highly recommended.
Schwab's CEO states that Gen Z clients (investors between the ages of 13 and 28) learn about finances primarily through social media and family.

FINRA research (published 2026-04-01) reports that 36 percent of social media users and 41 percent of finfluencer followers check the background, registration, or license of a financial professional with a state or federal regulator, versus 14 percent of non-users and 13 percent of non-followers.

In the 2025 Wealthtender Voice of the Client study (all survey respondents, not age-specific), the top financial goals or needs respondents would seek a financial advisor's help with are retirement planning and income strategies (63%), investment management and portfolio growth (53%), tax planning and optimization (29%), estate planning and wealth transfer (26%), debt management and reduction (16%), budgeting and cash flow management (14%), saving for a major purchase such as a home or business (13%), insurance needs and risk management (11%), and saving for children's education (10%).

For the next generation (UBS, published 2026-04-22), experience and expertise sit at the top of the wish list when choosing a wealth manager (79%), and more than half (56%) want advisors who can build trusted relationships across generations, while 41% value an advisor's ability to fully understand the next generation's needs.

Cerulli (published 2025-10-29) notes that Millennials have contended with heightened student debt and economic upheaval, and recent higher mortgage rates have put the goal of home ownership further out of reach for some; as a result, some Millennials have delayed traditional milestones such as getting married, buying a home, and having children.

By generation (GSAM, published 2025-10-17), the top three most important investment goals for Millennials are to grow wealth over time, plan for comfortable or early retirement, and achieve financial independence.

GSAM (published 2025-10-01) reports that competing financial priorities materially constrain retirement saving for approximately 30% of working Baby Boomers, rising to more than 50% for Gen X, exceeding 75% for Millennials, and remaining above 70% for Gen Z.

GSAM (published 2025-10-01) reports that the competing priorities affecting respondents' ability to save for retirement include credit card debt, paying down existing loans (student loans, etc.), saving for college, caring for and financially supporting family members, time out of the workforce, financial hardship, and too many monthly financial expenses; younger generations (Gen X, Millennials, Gen Z) report a significantly higher impact from these challenges than Baby Boomers, with Millennials the most impacted.
